common_name: Scarlet Gem Daffodil (Multi-Flowered Tazetta with Deep Orange Cups)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; an early-1900s tazetta hybrid bred in Cornwall that needs little winter chill and naturalizes well in mild-winter Southern gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Scarlet Gem was raised by Cornish hybridizer Percival D. Williams and registered before 1910, bearing clusters of golden-yellow, lightly fragrant flowers with small, deep orange-red cups, several to a stem. As a tazetta-type hybrid it requires very little winter chill compared with Dutch trumpet daffodils, blooming in early to midspring and naturalizing readily in the Gulf South's mild winters. Allow foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Laurens Koster Daffodil (Fragrant White Tazetta with Golden Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a 1906 Dutch tazetta known for strong fragrance and reliable naturalizing in low-chill Southern gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Laurens Koster was introduced in 1906 by Dutch grower A. Vis and bears four to five broad, rounded, creamy-white perianth segments around a shallow, bright orange-yellow cup, several flowers per stem with strong sweet fragrance. Like other old tazetta hybrids it needs minimal winter chill and has a long track record of naturalizing and multiplying in Southern gardens. Let foliage die back naturally after bloom and leave established clumps undisturbed.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum, NC State University

common_name: Double Campernelle Daffodil (Queen Anne's Double Jonquil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a centuries-old double jonquil pass-along plant long grown at Southern homesites under the name Queen Anne's Double Jonquil, distinct from the single-flowered Campernelle Jonquil already grown.

directions: Double Campernelle is a double-flowered sport of the old jonquil-trumpet hybrid Campernelle, known and grown in Europe since the 1500s-1600s and brought to American gardens very early, producing two to three fragrant, ruffled, rosebud-like golden-yellow blooms per rush-like stem. In the South it has long been called Queen Anne's Double Jonquil and, like single Campernelle, tolerates both cold winters and hot, humid summers with essentially no chill requirement, blooming as early as late February and naturalizing readily in lawns and rough grass. Allow foliage to die back naturally and leave clumps undisturbed to multiply for decades.

common_name: Texas Star Daffodil (Naturalized Southern Heirloom Jonquilla-Tazetta Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a natural jonquilla-tazetta hybrid pass-along daffodil found widely naturalized at old homesites across Texas and the Deep South.

directions: Texas Star is a naturally occurring hybrid between Narcissus jonquilla and Narcissus tazetta, bearing clusters of small, fragrant, pale yellow flowers in late winter to early spring. Despite its name it has been found naturalized across old homesites throughout the South, tolerating everything from heavy clay and wet ditches to dry sandy soil with essentially no winter chill requirement. It multiplies quickly by offsets into dense long-lived colonies; leave foliage to die back naturally and divide only when clumps become crowded.

common_name: Incomparable Daffodil (Historic Southern Heirloom Peerless Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a natural poeticus-pseudonarcissus hybrid first described in 1635 and long persistent at old Southern homesites.

directions: Incomparable is a natural hybrid between Narcissus poeticus and N. pseudonarcissus first described in 1635, once called the Great Nonsuch Daffodil for its then-unprecedented flower size, bearing a single soft-yellow perianth around a slightly deeper cup. It has persisted for generations in clumps around abandoned Southern homesites and under deciduous trees, blooming in early March in the mild lull between winter cold and spring rains. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize.

common_name: Early Louisiana Jonquil (Heirloom Extra-Early Fragrant Wild Jonquil Strain)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a vigorous, extra-early-blooming wild jonquil strain documented at old Louisiana homesites and preserved by Old House Gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Early Louisiana is a distinctly vigorous, unusually early-flowering strain of the wild jonquil Narcissus jonquilla, documented among old Louisiana homesites by plantsman Carl Amason and noted for a fragrance strong enough to perfume the garden on a warm night. It blooms clusters of small, deep-yellow, sweetly scented flowers weeks ahead of standard Dutch-grown jonquils and self-sows readily, requiring essentially no winter chill to perform well in Gulf South gardens. Allow foliage to die back naturally and leave clumps undisturbed to spread.

common_name: St. Keverne Daffodil (Reliable Heat-Tolerant Golden Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; an RHS Award of Garden Merit trumpet daffodil singled out as one of the most reliable heat- and humidity-tolerant Dutch-type daffodils for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: St. Keverne bears clear, uniform golden-yellow trumpet flowers and earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit in 1993 as well as the American Daffodil Society's Wister Award in 2007 for outstanding garden performance. It is named among the Gulf Coast's most dependable trumpet-type daffodils, returning and reblooming reliably where many other Dutch trumpet cultivars decline for lack of winter chill. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize.

common_name: Tenby Daffodil (Welsh Heirloom Dwarf Golden Trumpet Species Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a pre-1800 Welsh heirloom species daffodil with an RHS Award of Garden Merit that appears on Southern heat-loving daffodil lists despite its cool-climate origin.

directions: The Tenby Daffodil is a dwarf, single-flowered, deep golden-yellow trumpet species native to the area around Tenby, Wales, documented in cultivation since before 1800 and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit. It naturalizes freely in turf, multiplying slowly but steadily with almost no maintenance, and is included among Old House Gardens' top heat-tolerant picks for mild-winter Southern gardens. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or mowing over it.

common_name: Dick Wellband Daffodil (Historic Large-Cupped Daffodil with Deep Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; an early large-cupped daffodil noted for dense, long-lived clumps and inclusion on Southern heat-tolerant daffodil lists.

directions: Dick Wellband arose in the garden of English hybridizer Sarah Backhouse, was registered before 1921, and received the Haarlem Award of Merit in 1931 for its then-unusually deep, ruffled orange-red cup set against lustrous white-to-yellow petals. It forms exceptionally dense, crowd-tolerant clumps that keep flowering well even when congested, and is listed among the heat-loving daffodils recommended for Southern gardens. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom and leave established clumps largely undisturbed.

common_name: Italicus Daffodil (Heirloom Star-Shaped White Tazetta with Lemon Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; an old Mediterranean tazetta long cultivated in historic Spanish and French Gulf Coast settlements and one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often by January.

directions: Italicus bears clusters of star-shaped white perianth segments that hold their form without overlapping, surrounding a lemon-yellow cup, on a sweetly fragrant, multi-flowered stem similar in form to the Chinese Sacred Lily but with a paler cup. It is documented growing at old Spanish and French settlement sites across Louisiana and is one of the earliest daffodils to open, frequently blooming as early as January in the Deep South with essentially no chilling requirement. Allow foliage to die back naturally and leave clumps undisturbed, since it multiplies steadily into large, long-lived stands.
